title: Episode 1: The Assassins Who Weren't
chapters: How an Insult Became a Word
summary: Everyone has heard of the Assassins: drugged young men, a secret garden of paradise, and a sinister Old Man of the Mountain. Yusuf and Reem set Marco Polo's famous story against what the Ismaili community's own institutions actually publish. They cover the 1094 succession split in Cairo, Hasan-i Sabbah and the mountain fortress of Alamut, and the fidais treated honestly — the Nizaris did carry out targeted political killings, and the sources that say so also show how far the reputation outran the reality. They meet Rashid al-Din Sinan, the Syrian leader who talked Saladin into a truce and then had his title stolen by legend, and trace how a medieval insult became the English word "assassin". Then come the Mongols, Juwayni's claim that the community had been wiped out, the evidence that it hadn't, two centuries of quiet survival, and the line of Imams that runs down to Aga Khan V today.

title: Episode 2: Where It All Began
summary: The prequel. When the Prophet Muhammad died in 632, Muslims answered the question of who should guide the community in two different ways, and Yusuf and Reem start at the pond of Ghadir Khumm, where a single word — mawla — is read one way by Shia Muslims and another by everyone else. From there: Imam Ali and the party that formed around him, Hasan's treaty and the Ismaili view of his role, the killing of Husayn at Karbala and what it meant, and the quiet generations of teaching Imams — Zayn al-Abidin, Muhammad al-Baqir with his doctrine of nass, and Ja'far al-Sadiq — whose Imamate held no political power at all. Then the dispute of 765 over Ismail and Musa al-Kazim, how the Ismailis got a name they rarely used for themselves, and the long period of concealment that ends in a Syrian town called Salamiyya, from which a hidden Imam ran one of the most effective missions of the age. Along the way the hosts are honest about what the community's own institutions do not publish, which turns out to be a story in itself.

title: Episode 3: The Caliphs of Cairo
chapters: A Dynasty Looking For a Capital
summary: For two and a half centuries the Ismaili Imams were also caliphs, and they ruled from a city they built themselves. Yusuf and Reem follow the mission that made it possible, the rescue at Sijilmasa that brought the first Fatimid caliph out of concealment in nine oh nine, and the run of new capitals that ends with al-Muizz carrying his three dead predecessors across North Africa into Cairo. They look at the three very different classrooms of Fatimid Cairo — al-Azhar, open to everyone including women, the sessions of wisdom inside the palace, and the Dar al-Ilm with its four hundred thousand manuscripts — before turning to al-Hakim, the ruler who came to the throne at eleven, who has attracted more lurid legend than anyone else in the dynasty, and who rode into the hills one night in ten twenty-one and was never seen again. The episode ends with the long reign of al-Mustansir, the viziers of the sword, the split of ten ninety-four, and the very quiet end of the caliphate under Saladin in eleven seventy-one.

title: Episode 4: Reason and Revelation
chapters: The Man Who Became a Ruby
summary: A thousand years ago a scholar in Cairo looked at the Quran's six days of creation and pointed out that there was no sun yet — so what is a day? Yusuf and Reem spend the most abstract episode of the season chasing that habit of mind. They meet zahir and batin, the outward and inner meaning that Ismaili thought holds together like body and soul, and the practice of tawil that leads a text back to its root. They visit the Fatimid curriculum, where you learned the steps before you were told what the dance meant, and the Brethren of Purity, whose encyclopaedia put music and the soul in the same set of books and whose authorship nobody can settle. Reem says plainly that she finds one claim hard — that reason has a ceiling — and gets an honest answer rather than a tidy one. Then comes Nasir Khusraw, who lost his house, fled to a mountain valley, and wrote that he had been stone and became a ruby. The episode ends on the verse of light that gives the show its name, and on the part of that teaching the community keeps for itself.

title: Episode 5: Hidden in Plain Sight
chapters: Two Hundred Years of Not Much
The Mountains That Kept the Books
summary: The Mongols wrecked Alamut, a court historian declared the Ismailis exterminated, and for two centuries almost nobody contradicted him. Yusuf and Reem follow what actually happened next: taqiyya and satr, and why the community's own institutions present concealment as survival under persecution rather than deceit. They sit in the gap where the record nearly disappears, meet the Imams who re-emerged at Anjudan looking to everyone outside like Sufi masters, and find that a Shia state under the Safavids made things worse rather than better. Then two places that kept the tradition alive: the mountain valleys of Badakhshan, where families copied and hid the manuscripts modern scholarship depends on, and the Indian subcontinent, where the pirs built Satpanth in local languages and the ginans carried it in song. Along the way the hosts stop three times to say plainly that the community's institutions publish nothing on a question — and why that silence is worth hearing.

title: Episode 6: From Persia to Bombay
summary: The hiding stops. Yusuf and Reem follow the Ismaili Imams out of the Iranian villages and onto a much larger stage: a title handed over by a Persian king, a thirteen-year-old governor, an armed confrontation and a departure that ended seven centuries of the Imamat living in Persia. In Bombay the Imam finally has a fixed address, the Khoja merchant families of Gujarat and Kutch can reach him, and a dispute over communal property lands in the Bombay High Court in eighteen sixty-six — a case the hosts are careful to say we only know the outcome of. Then Aga Khan III: Imam at seven, seventy-two years in office, written constitutions from nineteen oh five, the presidency of the League of Nations Assembly, hundreds of schools, and the guidance that if a family could educate only one child it should be the daughter. It ends on the weighing ceremonies, what the jubilee gold actually built, and the will of nineteen fifty-seven that skipped a generation to a twenty-year-old student at Harvard.

title: Episode 7: The Development Imam
summary: A twenty-year-old student at Harvard becomes the 49th Ismaili Imam, and leads the community for sixty-seven years. Yusuf and Reem follow Aga Khan IV from his grandfather's will in 1957 to the expulsion of Uganda's Asian population in 1972 and the resettlement in Canada — being honest that the community's own institutions publish almost nothing about those weeks — then ask what the Aga Khan Development Network actually does, and why a spiritual office runs universities, hospitals and companies at all. They visit the architecture prize that pays the builders as well as the architect, the Aga Khan Museum in Toronto and the seven Ismaili Centres, and work out how a palace in Lisbon became the first formal Seat of the Imamat in its modern history. The episode closes with February 2025 — the death in Lisbon, the funeral, the burial at Aswan, the reading of the will and the Takht-nishini of Aga Khan V — and with the new Imam returning to Uganda to open a university campus.

title: Episode 8: A Day in the Life
summary: After seven episodes of caliphs, castles and development banks, Yusuf and Reem come down to the ordinary week. What a Jamatkhana actually is — the house of the community, a word the Ismailis share with Sunni Memons, Shia Bohras and Chishti Sufis — and how the whole family of Muslim gathering spaces grows out of a courtyard beside the Prophet's house in Medina. Who may go in, and why the formal congregational prayers are reserved for those who have pledged bayah, explained in the community's own words rather than ours. The forms of prayer and the devotional poetry, from the ginans of South Asia to the Persian qasida and Central Asian maddah-khani. The festival year, from Navroz to Laylat al-Qadr to the Imam's Salgirah. Didar, and the visit to Tajikistan that a family in Khorog wrote into a child's name. And the volunteers who run nearly all of it, under a motto the Imam gave them in nineteen twenty-four: "Work No Words". This is also the episode where the hosts keep stopping: the text of the Dua, the order of the ceremony, Baitul Khayal, Chiragh-i Rawshan, nandi and mehmani, and even the etiquette a guest might want are not published by the community's own institutions, and the show says so and leaves them alone.

title: Episode 9: Among the Muslims
chapters: The Legend and the Lost Library
summary: The season finale steps outside the community and looks at the neighbours. Yusuf and Reem start with the enormous shared ground — one God, the Prophet, the Quran — before following the fork at Ghadir Khumm and the second fork after Imam Jafar al-Sadiq that separated Ismailis from Twelver Shias. They walk the rest of the family tree, the Mustali Tayyibis and the Bohras, the Druze and the Imam-Shahis, and they are blunt throughout that every source here is an Ismaili institution describing other communities rather than those communities speaking for themselves. Then come a thousand years of living alongside Sunni Muslims, in both directions: the Abbasid campaigns and the Seljuq massacres, but also Fatimid religious plurality and the Imam at Alamut who won recognition from the caliph in Baghdad. The episode closes with Daftary's 'black legend', the Baghdad declaration of 1011, the manuscripts that came out of hiding in the twentieth century — many of them preserved by the Bohras — the Amman consensus on the eight schools, and a warm look back across the season.
